extracted.intended_audience: Attorneys and parties in inter partes proceedings before the TTAB (Trademark Trial and Appeal Board)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on discovery practice in inter partes TTAB trademark proceedings, covering requests for production and admission, ESI production, discovery conferences, disclosures (including experts), signatures/certifications, duties to cooperate, and sanctions. Applies to cases governed by 37 C.F.R. §2.120 and the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure as adopted by the Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board authority over place/manner/form of production
rubrics_metrics.description: On motion pursuant to 37 CFR § 2.120(d)(2), the Board may by order specify the place and the manner in which the documents are to be produced, and in situations involving electronically stored information, the form of production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the Board may order the responding party to photocopy designated documents and mail photocopies when the responding party has unreasonably refused to produce documents. See related case citations and notes for sanctions and cost-allocation examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to each item of a request for production
rubrics_metrics.description: For each item or category, the response must either state that inspection and related activities will be permitted as requested or state an objection to the request, including the reasons (Fed. R. Civ. P. 34(b)(2)(B)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If objection is made to only part of an item or category, the part must be specified (Fed. R. Civ. P. 34(b)(2)(C)). A proper response should state whether responsive documents exist and, if so, whether they will be produced or withheld on a claim of privilege. It is generally inappropriate to attack requests by filing motions instead of responding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objections and form-of-production for ESI
rubrics_metrics.description: A response to a request for production of electronically stored information may state an objection to a requested form for producing ESI; if the responding party objects to a requested form — or if no form was specified — the party must state the form or forms it intends to use (Fed. R. Civ. P. 34(b)(2)(D)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no form specified, party must produce ESI in the form in which it is ordinarily maintained, or in a reasonably usable form. If the request specifies a form and no objection is made, the responding party must produce the information in that form. Parties should attempt to resolve form issues during the discovery conference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production as kept in the usual course or organized/labelled
rubrics_metrics.description: A party that produces documents for inspection must produce them as they are kept in the usual course of business, or must organize and label them to correspond with the categories in the request (Fed. R. Civ. P. 34(b)(2)(E)(i)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party may not simply 'dump' large quantities of documents containing responsive as well as unresponsive documents. Organize and label productions to correspond with request categories to facilitate review.

rubrics_metrics.name: ESI production protocols to discuss
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspects of ESI production other than form that should be discussed include a protocol for identifying and segregating potentially responsive ESI, who should review the ESI to determine appropriateness of production, and methods of searching the ESI (e.g., keywords).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These topics should be discussed at the discovery conference or when it becomes apparent ESI will be produced. See case law cited for guidance on efficient methods and expectations (e.g., exchanging copies vs. identifying locations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not substitute motion practice for responses
rubrics_metrics.description: It is generally inappropriate for a party to respond to requests for production by filing a motion attacking them (e.g., motion to strike, suppress, or protective order); the party should ordinarily respond by indicating inspection will be permitted for proper requests and stating reasons for objection for improper ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See TBMP §410. Motions should not replace answering and objecting as required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time to respond to requests for admission
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses to requests for admission must be served within 30 days after the date of service of the requests (37 C.F.R. § 2.120(a)(3); Fed. R. Civ. P. 36(a)(3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If served by first-class mail/Express Mail/overnight courier, date of mailing/delivery is date of service and five extra days are allowed. If parties agreed to electronic service (fax/email), no additional time is allowed. Under Fed. R. Civ. P. 36, a matter is admitted unless answered or objected to within 30 days.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of failure to timely respond to requests for admission
rubrics_metrics.description: A requested admission is deemed admitted unless, within 30 days after being served, the party serves a written answer or objection; admissions by failure to respond are conclusive unless excusable neglect is shown or a motion to withdraw/amend is granted (Fed. R. Civ. P. 36(a)(3), 36(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary to file a motion to deem requests admitted when no response is served; admissions occur by operation of law. For relief, see TBMP §525 and case law on excusable neglect and motions under Rule 36(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and form requirements of requests for admission
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests for admission may seek truth of matters within the scope of Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(1), including (A) facts, application of law to fact, or opinions; and (B) genuineness of described documents. Each matter must be separately stated; a request to admit genuineness must be accompanied by a copy of the document unless it has been made available (Fed. R. Civ. P. 36(a)(1)-(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests for admission are particularly useful to determine facts not in dispute and to facilitate introduction into evidence of documents produced by adversary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive nature of answers to requests for admission
rubrics_metrics.description: If a matter is not admitted, the answer must specifically deny it or state in detail why the answering party cannot truthfully admit or deny it. A denial must fairly respond to the substance; when qualifying or denying part of a matter, specify the part admitted and qualify or deny the rest. Lack of knowledge may be asserted only after reasonable inquiry (Fed. R. Civ. P. 36(a)(4)-(5)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If objecting, state grounds for objection; may not object solely because the matter presents a genuine issue for trial — instead deny or explain inability to admit. The Board prefers reproducing each request immediately before the answer/objection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature/certification requirements and consequences (Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: By signing, an attorney or party certifies that, to the best of the person's knowledge after reasonable inquiry: (A) disclosures are complete and correct as of the time made; and (B) discovery requests, responses, and objections are warranted, not interposed for improper purpose, and neither unreasonable nor unduly burdensome considering needs of the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The signature constitutes a certification subject to sanctions if violated. The certification duty requires reasonable inquiry into factual basis. The signature also means a party ordinarily cannot later claim a request is proper when propounded by one party but improper when propounded by another, absent persuasive reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to cooperate in discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties and their attorneys/authorized representatives have a duty to cooperate in the discovery process and to make a good faith effort to satisfy the reasonable and appropriate discovery needs of their adversary and to seek only discovery proper and relevant to the issues (Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(g) referenced).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board looks with extreme disfavor on non-cooperation; failure to cooperate may lead to sanctions, estoppel, or judgment. Duty to cooperate continues despite an adversary's failure to fulfill obligations. Case law examples illustrate sanctions for uncooperative or oppressive discovery conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to conduct discovery conference
rubrics_metrics.description: For cases commenced on or after November 1, 2007, parties are required to hold a conference to discuss settlement and plans for discovery. The conference should address the nature/basis of claims and defenses, possibility of settlement, plans for disclosures and discovery, Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f) subjects, and any Board-required subjects in the institution order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere discussion of settlement does not substitute for full discovery conference. Parties must discuss plans for disclosures, discovery and trial evidence unless the case settles. See TBMP §401.01 for more detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and procedures when a party refuses to participate in discovery conference
rubrics_metrics.description: All parties have a duty to cooperate and conduct the discovery conference in a timely fashion. If a party refuses to cooperate, the scheduling party should contact the assigned Board attorney; the Board may set a date and warn the non-cooperating party that failure to participate may lead to sanctions including judgment (37 C.F.R. §2.120(g)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A motion to compel participation is not prerequisite to a motion for sanctions; however, the moving party must show a good faith effort to schedule the conference. The Board may order the uncooperative party to show cause why judgment should not be entered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to make initial disclosures and expert disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Each party is obliged to make initial disclosures by the deadline in the Board’s institution order (intended to disclose names of potential witnesses and basic information about documents/things the party may use). Expert disclosures must be served 30 days prior to the close of discovery (Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(2) per 37 C.F.R. §2.120(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial disclosures are intended to reduce surprise and streamline discovery. Expert disclosures may be extensive and need not be filed with the Board, but parties should inform the Board when an expert disclosure is made so the Board can issue appropriate orders (e.g., suspend proceedings to allow necessary expert discovery). Parties should discuss expert testimony during the discovery conference and revisit as necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion to compel must show good-faith effort to resolve disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion to compel initial disclosures, expert testimony disclosures, or discovery must be supported by a written statement that the moving party has made a good faith effort, by conference or correspondence, to resolve the issues but was unable to do so (37 C.F.R. §2.120(e)(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document the meet-and-confer efforts; failure to do so may result in denial of the motion. See related TBMP provisions for meet-and-confer expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect and scope of admissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Any matter admitted (expressly or by failure to timely respond) under Fed. R. Civ. P. 36(a) is conclusively established for the pending proceeding unless the Board permits withdrawal/amendment or reopens time to respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An admission is only for the purpose of the pending proceeding and cannot be used against the party in other proceedings. Admissions cannot generally be rebutted by contrary testimony at trial unless withdrawn or amended per Rule 36(b) and Board order; case law provides examples where relief was or was not granted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks of attorney signature on responses to requests for admission
rubrics_metrics.description: Answers and objections to requests for admission may be signed by the responding party or its attorney; however, an attorney who signs answers or objections risks becoming a witness or disqualification from representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Care should be taken before counsel signs admissions/responses; consider who has personal knowledge and the potential conflict if counsel must testify. See 37 C.F.R. §10.63 and cited case law for consequences.
